query_text: how do you type up minutes of a meeting

parts.text:
Typing up meeting minutes is all about creating a clear, objective, and easy-to-read record of what happened during a meeting. You don't need to write down every single word said; instead, focus on **decisions made, actions to be taken, and key discussion points**.

Here is a step-by-step guide on how to type up professional meeting minutes, including a standard template you can use.

---

### Step 1: Use a Standard Structure
A professional set of meeting minutes should always include the following elements. You can copy and paste this structure into a Word document or Google Doc as your template:

> **[Name of Organization or Committee]**  
> **[Type of Meeting – e.g., Monthly Board Meeting, Weekly Marketing Sync]**  
> **Meeting Minutes**  
>
> * **Date:** [Date of the meeting]
> * **Time:** [Start time] to [End time]
> * **Location:** [Physical location or video call link, e.g., Zoom]
> * **Chairperson:** [Name of the person leading the meeting]
> * **Secretary/Minute-Taker:** [Your name]
>
> **1. Attendees**  
> * **Present:** [List names of all attendees]
> * **Apologies/Absent:** [List names of those who couldn't make it]
> * **Guests:** [List any guest speakers, if applicable]
>
> **2. Approval of Previous Minutes**  
> * [State whether the minutes from the last meeting were approved, approved with corrections, or postponed.]
> * *Example: "The minutes of the previous meeting on October 12th were approved as distributed."*
>
> **3. Agenda Topics & Discussion**  
> *(Create a section for each major topic discussed)*
> * **Topic 1: [Topic Name]**
>     * **Discussion:** A brief, objective summary of the key points raised. Avoid listing who said what unless it is crucial for context. 
>     * **Decision:** [State any decisions made. If a formal vote was taken, record it here, e.g., "Motion approved 5-2."]
>     * **Action Item:** [Who is doing what, and by when?]
>
> **4. New Business**  
> * [Record any unexpected topics that were brought up and how they were addressed.]
>
> **5. Next Meeting**  
> * **Date & Time:** [Date and time of the next scheduled meeting]
> * **Location:** [Location or virtual link]
>
> **6. Adjournment**  
> * The meeting was adjourned at [Time] by [Name of Chairperson].
>
> **Submitted by:** [Your Name, Title]  
> **Date of Submission:** [Date you finished typing the minutes]

---

### Step 2: Write with the Right Tone and Style
When translating your handwritten or typed rough notes into the final document, follow these professional writing standards:

* **Be objective and neutral:** Write in an unbiased, third-person tone. Avoid emotional language, personal opinions, or capturing arguments. 
  * *Bad:* "John angrily argued that the budget was too small, but Sarah shut him down."
  * *Good:* "The committee discussed the limitations of the current budget. It was agreed to explore alternative funding sources."
* **Focus on actions and decisions:** The most critical parts of the minutes are **what was decided** and **who is responsible for what**. 
* **Use the past tense:** Write the minutes in the past tense (e.g., "The board approved," "The team discussed").
* **Keep summaries brief:** You do not need to transcribe the entire conversation. Summarize the general consensus of a discussion in 2 to 4 bullet points.

---

### Step 3: Format Action Items Clearly
The number one reason people read meeting minutes is to see what they need to do next. Make action items stand out so they are impossible to miss. 

* **Use bold text** for names and deadlines.
* Use a bulleted list or a table at the end of the document to summarize all action items.

> **Example Action Item Format:**
> * **Action:** Design the new homepage layout.
> * **Assigned to:** Sarah Jenkins
> * **Deadline:** November 15, 2026

---

### Step 4: Review and Edit
Before you send the minutes out, do a quick self-edit:
* **Check spelling and names:** Ensure everyone's name is spelled correctly.
* **Clarity check:** Read it through and ask yourself, *"If someone missed this meeting, would they understand exactly what happened and what the next steps are?"*
* **Keep it concise:** Delete fluff, repetitive statements, or off-topic chatter.

---

### Step 5: Distribute and File
1. **Send for approval:** Depending on your organization, you may need to send the draft to the Chairperson or your manager for review before sharing it with the wider group.
2. **Distribute quickly:** Try to send out the minutes within **24 to 48 hours** while the meeting is still fresh in everyone’s mind.
3. **File them safely:** Save the document as a PDF with a clear naming convention (e.g., `2026-11-05_Marketing_Meeting_Minutes.pdf`) and upload it to your team's shared drive or archiving system.
